Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026)
Per Curiam
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
No. 26A560
MARKWAYNE MULLIN, SECRETARY OF HOMELAND
SECURITY, ET AL. v. FRIENDS OF THE
RUIDOSA CHURCH, ET AL.
ON APPLICATION FOR STAY
[November 9, 2026]
 PER CURIAM.
Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immi­
grant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secre­
tary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct bor­
der barriers and roads “to deter illegal crossings in areas of
high illegal entry into the United States.”  §102(a), 110 Stat.
3009–554, as amended, note following 8 U. S. C. §1103.  The
same section expressly authorizes the Secretary “‘to waive
all legal requirements’” as “‘necessary to ensure expedi­
tious construction’” of those barriers and roads, §102(c)(1),
119 Stat. 306, and sharply limits judicial review of all
claims arising from such waiver determinations.  Specifi­
cally, the statute provides that “‘[a] cause of action or claim
may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution
of the United States’” and courts “‘shall not have jurisdic­
tion’” over nonconstitutional claims.  §102(c)(2)(A).
Earlier this year, the Secretary invoked Section 102’s
waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at
the U. S.–Mexico border, in a region that U. S. Customs and
Border Protection has designated the “Big Bend Sector.”
The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector “is an area of
high illegal entry” requiring additional border barriers, and
waived the application of a variety of environmental and
conservation laws to facilitate expeditious construction.

2
MULLIN v. FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH
Per Curiam
See 91 Fed. Reg. 7298 (2026), as amended by id., at 40550;
id., at 27969, as amended by id., at 34831; id., at 46939.
Shortly thereafter, respondents—an individual river
guide, an environmental nonprofit, and a nonprofit organi­
zation dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa,
Texas—challenged those waiver determinations by filing
suit in the U. S. District Court for the Western District of
Texas. Respondents claimed, among other things, that the
Secretary’s waiver determinations “violat[ed] the major
questions doctrine under the U. S. Constitution, Article I,
Section 1.” First Amended Complaint in No. 3:26–cv–01099
(WD Tex.), ECF Doc. 26, ¶¶75–85 (some capitalization
omitted).
Although styled as constitutional, that claim
simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory
authority in issuing the waivers. Ibid.
On October 2, 2026, the District Court entered a prelimi­
nary injunction blocking the Secretary’s waivers and halt­
ing all associated construction.  The District Court acknowl­
edged that its jurisdiction was limited to constitutional
claims. But it nonetheless concluded that respondents’
“major questions doctrine claim” qualified because, in its
view, the “major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear
statement rule grounded in separation of powers.”  Memo­
randum Opinion in No. 3:26–cv–01099 (WD Tex.), ECF Doc.
75, at 7–8. The court further held that respondents’ “major
questions doctrine claim” was likely to succeed on the mer­
its because the Secretary lacked “‘clear congressional au­
thorization’ to issue” the waivers. Id., at 8. Because the
Fifth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear this case, IIRIRA
§102(c)(2)(C), the Solicitor General filed an application re­
questing either summary reversal or a stay of the District
Court’s preliminary injunction.
We grant the requested stay. The Government is exceed­
ingly likely to prevail on its argument that the District
Court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate respondents’ so-
called major-questions-doctrine claim.
However it is

3
Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026)
Per Curiam
labeled, respondents’ claim does not “‘alleg[e] a violation of
the Constitution of the United States,’” the only type of
claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate.
IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(A). It alleges instead that the Secretary
exceeded his statutory authority.  And we have long recog­
nized that “claims simply alleging” that the Executive
Branch has exceeded its “statutory authority are not ‘con­
stitutional’ claims.” Dalton v. Specter, 511 U. S. 462, 472–
474 (1994).
That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plain­
tiff invokes the major-questions doctrine.  Many canons and
rules of statutory interpretation reflect constitutional prin­
ciples, including “constitutional avoidance, the clear-state­
ment federalism rules, and the presumption against retro-
activity.” Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U. S. 477, 508 (2023)
(BARRETT, J., concurring). When courts invoke those can­
ons, however, they do so in service of adjudicating statutory
claims, not constitutional ones. See Clark v. Martinez, 543
U. S. 371, 382 (2005) (explaining that litigants invoke the
constitutional-avoidance canon to vindicate their “statutory
rights”).  The same is true when a court invokes “the major
questions canon of statutory interpretation.”  FCC v. Con­
sumers’ Research, 606 U. S. 656, 705 (2025) (KAVANAUGH,
J., concurring).  There is no such thing as a “constitutional”
major-questions claim.
The remaining factors also warrant a stay.  To start, the
District Court’s order, which bars the Secretary from exer­
cising his statutory authority to waive applicable laws as he
“determines necessary to ensure expeditious construction”
of border barriers under IIRIRA §102(c)(1), delays the Gov­
ernment’s construction of border barriers and roads in the
Big Bend Sector.  The injunction thus impedes the Govern­
ment from advancing its “compelling interests” in border
security and integrity. Treasury Employees v. Von Raab,
489 U. S. 656, 672 (1989); see App. to Application 226a, ¶5.

4
MULLIN v. FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH
Per Curiam
In addition, the Government has presented a declaration
from a U. S. Customs and Border Protection official, who
attests that—because of the injunction—the Government is
incurring nearly half a million dollars in costs per day,
which “cannot be recouped” if it prevails at the end of this
litigation. Id., 222a, ¶20–22. “[W]hile the loss of money is
not typically considered irreparable harm, that changes if
the funds cannot be recouped and are thus irrevocably ex­
pended.” National Institutes of Health v. American Public
Health Assn., 606 U. S. 998 (2025) (internal quotation
marks omitted).
The balance of the equities also favors the Government.
Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector
will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area.  But
Congress’s enactment of IIRIRA §102(c)—which permits
the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-
protection and other conservation laws—reflects a clear
preference for expeditious border construction over the very
harms respondents assert. §102(c)(1).  And courts “of equity
cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress
has struck in a statute.” United States v. Oakland Canna­
bis Buyers’ Coop., 532 U. S. 483, 497 (2001). The Govern­
ment’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recrea­
tional, and environmental harm alleged by respondents.
See Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 555
U. S. 7, 25–26 (2008).
*
*
*
The application for stay presented to JUSTICE ALITO and
by him referred to the Court is granted.  The injunction en­
tered by the United States District Court for the Western
District of Texas in case No. 3:26–cv–01099 is stayed pend­
ing the filing and disposition of the Government’s petition
for a writ of certiorari, if such writ is timely sought.  Should
certiorari be denied, this stay shall terminate automati­
cally. In the event certiorari is granted, the stay shall

terminate upon the sending down of the judgment of this
Court.
It is so ordered.
 JUSTICE JACKSON would deny the application for stay.
